concept.name: Anti-money-laundering controls
concept.definition: The program of internal policies, procedures, and controls that financial institutions must establish to guard against money laundering and the financing of terrorism. Under 31 U.S.C. § 5318(h) each financial institution must maintain an AML program including, at a minimum, internal policies/procedures/controls, a designated compliance officer, ongoing employee training, and an independent audit function, applied on a risk basis.
concept.intuition: Banks and brokers must build a filter that makes it hard to wash dirty money through the financial system — and prove to examiners that the filter actually works.
concept.mechanics: An AML program combines the four statutory pillars (controls, compliance officer, training, independent testing) with customer due diligence/KYC, transaction monitoring, suspicious activity reporting (SARs under § 5318(g)), currency transaction reporting, and recordkeeping under the Bank Secrecy Act. Institutions must direct more resources to higher-risk customers and activities and face examination by their functional regulators.
concept.failure_modes: Controls calibrated to catch known typologies miss novel laundering methods (trade-based laundering, crypto mixing, nested correspondent accounts); programs also drown analysts in low-quality alerts, and institutions sometimes de-risk entire customer categories rather than manage the risk.
concept.misconceptions: AML compliance is not just filing SARs — the statute requires a risk-based program with governance, training, and independent testing; and it applies beyond banks to broker-dealers, futures commission merchants, mutual funds, and money services businesses.
concept.example: A broker-dealer's monitoring system flags a customer who wires in $900,000 from a high-risk jurisdiction and immediately buys and liquidates securities with minimal trading rationale; the firm investigates and files a SAR with FinCEN.
